title: From handwork to the factory
question: How did new machines, power and iron change how things were made?
hook: Mechanised cotton spinning raised output per worker by a factor of around 500.
idea: Machines, steam and water power and new iron processes moved production from hand to factory and set off lasting growth in population and income.

beats.prompt: Cotton spinning is mechanised and powered first by water, then by steam. About how much more does each worker produce?

choices.label: A few percent more, since machines mostly save effort
choices.feedback: Machines can sound like small tweaks, but the gain was far larger than a few percent.

choices.label: About double, like adding a second pair of hands
choices.feedback: Doubling sounds big, but the real gain was hundreds of times.

beats.explain: Mechanised cotton spinning powered by water, and later steam, increased output per worker by a factor of around 500.

beats.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: The cast iron blowing cylinder is first used
A French envoy writes of an industrial revolution
Hot blast is developed to save fuel in iron-making
Engels writes of an industrial revolution in his book on English workers
beats.explain: The blowing cylinder dates to 1760, the phrase was first recorded in 1799, hot blast was developed in 1828 and Engels wrote in 1844.

beats.prompt: Match each machine or process to its gain.
pairs: Output per worker up around 500 times
Output up by a factor of 40
beats.explain: Each one multiplied what a worker or a process could do.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?
steps: Mechanised spinning was adopted rapidly in Britain in the 1780s.
Steam power and iron production grew fast after 1800.
In the late 1830s growth carried on at the same pace, as markets kept expanding.
Rapid growth returned after 1870 with new innovations.
beats.explain: From the late 1830s growth slowed because adoption of early innovations slowed as markets matured.
